newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan President Rabbani pushes for negotiation.
newsitem.headline: Afghan President Rabbani pushes for negotiation.

text.p: Afghan President Burhanuddin Rabbani pleaded on Wednesday for negotiation, not confrontation, with insurgent Taleban forces who drove him and his government from Kabul and now control two-thirds of the country.

Speaking to reporters just west of Mazar-i-Sharif in northern Afghanistan, Rabbani sounded almost meek by comparison with remarks to reporters in Pol-e-Khomri on Monday when he vowed to take the offensive against the Taleban.
"We do not support more war. Everything possible should be achieved through negotiation," the Afghan president told reporters on Wednesday.

Rabbani arrived in Mazar-i-Sharif on Tuesday for his first meeting in three years with Uzbek strongman General Abdul Rashid Dostum, whose military and political support is needed to stem the Taleban tide now lapping northern Afghanistan.
The president said his aim was to form a broad-based and united front against the Taleban and that he had invited all factions to join him in an effort to reunify the country.
"Our first aim is restore security to the country and to stop the fighting. We are trying to create understanding and communication among all the ethnic groups," Rabbani said.
"This has been told to the Taleban too. If they don't agree then maybe the front will have to make some military and political decisions too."
It remained unclear on Wednesday whether Rabbani had invited Dostum to join the government or whether the Uzbek general would accept if invited.
Dostum left the Rabbani government in 1994 after crossing swords with Afghan defence minister Ahmad Shah Masood.

Masood, who withdrew from Kabul with Rabbani when it fell to the Taleban two weeks ago, is among the other factional leaders expected to arrive in Mazar-i-Sharif this week to see if an anti-Taleban alliance can be formed.
Some who observed Rabbani on Tuesday found his plan for a united front and his emphasis on negotiation vague responses in the face of a dire threat.
"Dostum does not need Rabbani to negotiate a deal with the Taleban," said one Dostum supporter listening to Rabbani.

"Rabbani needs Dostum to give his government a chance to survive. I'm surprised Rabbani had nothing new to say. His statements won't interest the Taleban. It's the same approach he had been following and which has him begging Dostum and fleeing Taleban."
Rabbani rejected any notion of a federation with the Taleban whereby Afghanistan would comprise a northern and a southern state inside its internationally recognised borders.
He said the goal should be a united Afghanistan, with no divisions, for the sake of the country and its neighbours.
"The breaking up of Afghanistan could also lead to the breaking up of Pakistan," he said.
Rabbani said Taleban advances into the mouth of the Pansjher Valley had been stopped and the insurgents had also lost in fighting south of the Salang Pass.
"Taleban have been defeated fully there and they have lost a lot of men," he said.
